###### Abstract

LLM agents’ capabilities depend not only on their underlying models but
also on their execution harnesses. Recursive self-improvement (RSI)
offers a promising approach to automatically evolve these harnesses.
However, deploying RSI in open-world settings still faces two critical
challenges. First, open-world tasks are typically unseen during the
harness design phase and novel at test time, leaving no ground-truth
verifiers to reliably guide online harness edits. Second, the RSI
process remains highly task-specific and fails to generalize to novel
scenarios. We introduce Harness², a plug-and-play, _recursive agent
harnessing_ framework that addresses these challenges through two
connected levels of recursion. _Task-level recursion_ refines the
current task’s harness using a contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step
that reliably guides edits without ground-truth verifiers, and can be
scaled further via parallel or sequential recursion. _Harnessing-level
recursion_ then extracts experience from these edits to update a
continual improvement harness, enabling the agent to better adapt to
future tasks. Across three professional benchmarks and four
model–harness configurations, a single step consistently improves GLM-5
and Gemini 3.5 Flash over their base harnesses, yielding gains of up to
11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 4.5 points on JobBench, and 11.8
percentage points on LAB, with further gains as the task-level recursion
budget increases.

## 1 Introduction

An LLM agent’s effectiveness depends not only on its underlying model,
but also on its _harness_: the prompts, memory, skills, tools, and
orchestration through which the model performs tasks ([OpenAI,
2025](#bib.bib32); [SST, 2024](#bib.bib31); [Weng, 2026](#bib.bib1)).
Even a strong model can perform substantially differently under
different harnesses ([Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)). As agents expand
beyond coding into office workflows and high-stakes domains such as
legal work, harness design must accommodate increasingly diverse tasks
and operational requirements ([Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib9); [Harvey
AI, 2026](#bib.bib21)). Manually designing and refining harnesses for
these demands requires repeated engineering effort, motivating recursive
self-improvement on harness design ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7); [Lin
et al., 2026](#bib.bib16); [Qian et al., 2026](#bib.bib8); [Weng,
2026](#bib.bib1); [Meng et al., 2026](#bib.bib46)). Recursive
self-improvement (RSI) pursues AI that improves AI: a system
autonomously makes persistent changes to itself, and these changes
further shape how later improvements are generated, evaluated, and
retained ([Duan et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)).

Early harness RSI methods ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7); [Lin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)) focus on optimizing candidate components against
fixed training tasks, unit tests, or validation feedback, selecting the
best configuration before deployment. However, a static harness selected
beforehand often fails to generalize to the diverse, unpredictable
environments encountered in the open world ([Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib15)), a dynamic setting where agents continually
encounter new tasks with diverse and evolving requirements. To address
this, researchers have moved harness RSI to the _open world_, allowing
systems to dynamically adapt to newly arriving tasks. Current open-world
methods typically address this by recursively improving a harness for
the current task ([Lee et al., 2026a](#bib.bib17); [Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib15)), or by carrying a successful execution harness
forward across successive task batches ([Nie et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib18)).

However, open-world harness evolution faces two connected challenges.
First, tasks typically lack ground-truth labels or reliable verifiers.
While existing methods rely on proxy signals, assumed ground truth
answers, or pairwise output judgments ([Lee et al., 2026a](#bib.bib17);
[Nie et al., 2026b](#bib.bib18); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)), safely
using imperfect execution evidence to guide harness changes remains
difficult. Second, improving a harness for one task does not
automatically improve how the next task is refined. Task-specific edits
often fail when requirements change, and directly inheriting a highly
tailored execution harness can cause noisy recursive improvement as task
distributions shift. The refinement process itself, however, produces
highly reusable experience: how a weakness is diagnosed, which changes
are tested, and what their execution reveals. Therefore, the improvement
process itself must become a source of learning, enabling the system to
recursively upgrade its own refinement mechanism. This leads to our
central question:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To this end, we introduce Harness², a plug-and-play framework for
_recursive agent harnessing_ in an open world. We use _harnessing_ to
describe the process of optimizing the runtime scaffolding around a
frozen base model to enable it to act as an autonomous agent. Harness²
improves the harness for the current task and extracts lessons from that
process to guide future harnessing. It implements these updates through
two coupled levels of recursion: ❶ Task-level recursion refines the
current task’s _execution harness_. To overcome the absence of
ground-truth feedback, we introduce a contrastive
_Propose–Probe–Compose_ step: it proposes harness edits, tests their
effects under matched conditions, and composes changes supported by
behavioral contrasts. Building on this, _parallel recursion_ explores
multiple candidates simultaneously and composes changes from their
execution evidence, while _sequential recursion_ builds successive
revisions iteratively. ❷ Harnessing-level recursion uses the resulting
task-level explorations to update a _continual improvement harness_.
Instead of inheriting the previous execution harness, this improver
selectively retains reusable components and lessons about when and why
they worked, guiding future proposals and composition.

We evaluate Harness² on WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench, and Harvey’s Legal
Agent Benchmark ([Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib9); [Li et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20); [Harvey AI, 2026](#bib.bib21)) across four
executor–harness configurations. One contrastive step improves
performance on all three benchmarks in every configuration, with gains
of up to $`11.5`$ points on WorkBuddy-Bench, $`4.5`$ points on JobBench,
and $`11.8`$ percentage points in LAB Partial pass rate. Parallel
recursion adds up to $`3.9`$ points on WorkBuddy-Bench, $`4.2`$ on
JobBench, and $`6.7`$ percentage points on LAB Partial (Figure
[1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World"));
the budget study shows gains from both parallel and sequential
recursion. Importantly, task-level exploration also benefits subsequent
harnessing. Libraries accumulated with a larger recursion budget support
stronger subsequent harness edits even without additional probing, and a
library transferred from JobBench improves performance on
WorkBuddy-Bench (Figure
[7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")).
Our contributions are threefold:

- ①
  Recursive agent harnessing: Harness² refines the current execution
  harness and learns from the refinement process to guide future
  harnessing.
- ②
  Task-level recursion without ground-truth feedback: We introduce a
  contrastive Propose–Probe–Compose step that supports both parallel and
  sequential recursion.
- ③
  Experimental results: We demonstrate consistent gains across three
  benchmarks and four executor–harness configurations, including
  settings where the same model serves as both executor and editor.

## 2 Harness²

We first define recursive agent harnessing and its open-world setting
(§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Recursive Agent Harnessing ‣ 2 Harness2 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")).
We then present task-level recursion for refining the execution harness
(§[2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Task-Level Recursion ‣ 2 Harness2 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")),
followed by harnessing-level recursion for updating the improvement
harness across tasks
(§[2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Harnessing-Level Recursion ‣ 2 Harness2 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")).

### 2.1 Recursive Agent Harnessing

Harness Configuration and Setting. Let $`\mathcal{M}`$ be a model with
frozen parameters. A _harness_ $`\mathcal{H}=(c^{1},\ldots,c^{K})`$
consists of $`K`$ editable components, with $`c^{i}`$ denoting component
$`i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}`$. It composes with $`\mathcal{M}`$ to form an
agent $`\mathcal{A}(\cdot;\mathcal{M},\mathcal{H})`$ without changing
its weights ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7); [Huang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib10); [Qian et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)). For the execution
harness, we adopt the file-level decomposition of AHE ([Lin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)) and extend it by one component, exposing $`K=8`$
components: a system prompt, guardrails, memory, skills, tool guidance,
scripts, subagents, and a middleware plugin. Each component is mounted
as a file in the runtime. Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
shows their runtime roles, and Table
[5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.3 Editable Harness Components ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
in Appendix
[D.3](#A4.SS3 "D.3 Editable Harness Components ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
lists their files, activation, and definitions. We study harness
evolution over a stream of $`N`$ open-world tasks
$`q_{1},\ldots,q_{N}`$, without ground-truth answers or labeled
validation feedback. Each task starts from the common execution harness
$`\mathcal{H}_{0}`$. The pipeline may rerun the current task within a
bounded budget before returning its final deliverable.

Recursive Agent Harnessing. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is the
capability of an AI system to turn execution outcomes and internal
reflections into persistent changes to itself, such that these changes
also affect how later improvements are generated, evaluated, and
retained ([Duan et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)). The object of such changes
varies: model weights, as in self-rewarding language models ([Yuan et
al., 2024](#bib.bib48)); improvement programs, as in STOP ([Zelikman et
al., 2024](#bib.bib2)); and agent code, as in the Darwin Gödel Machine
([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib3)). The agent harness can be such an
object as well. It is the system surrounding a base model that enables
it to act as an autonomous agent
($`\text{Agent}=\text{Model}+\text{Harness}`$), without changing the
model weights ([Weng, 2026](#bib.bib1)). We call the process of
optimizing this layer _harnessing_. Rather than only revising an
execution harness under a fixed improvement procedure ([Lee et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib17); [Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7)), we also update the
harness guiding future revisions:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Recursive agent harnessing thus extends the model–harness view from an
agent that executes tasks to an agent that also learns how to improve
its harness: the execution harness is the system being improved, and the
improvement harness is the mechanism that improves it. In Harness², as
shown in Figure
[3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2.2.1 A Contrastive Improvement Step ‣ 2.2 Task-Level Recursion ‣ 2 Harness2 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World"),
the _execution harness_ is refined for the current task, while the
_continual improvement harness_ supports refinement across tasks. The
improvement harness remains fixed during task-level recursion and is
updated afterward through its _harness improvement library_. This
library retains adopted harnesses together with lessons from their
refinement, making both available for reuse and adaptation in subsequent
proposals and composition.

### 2.2 Task-Level Recursion

Task-level recursion aims to improve the execution harness for the
current task. The challenge in our open-world setting is to guide
revisions without ground-truth feedback. We therefore introduce a
_contrastive improvement step_ that proposes changes, executes them, and
examines their behavioral consequences. Building on this step, parallel
and sequential recursion use the generated harnesses and execution
evidence for further refinement.

#### 2.2.1 A Contrastive Improvement Step

![Refer to caption](2610.14224v1/harness2_main_new.png)

Figure 3: The Harness² pipeline. Task-level recursion proposes invariant
and domain-specific harness edits, probes their effects, and composes a
successor execution harness. After each task, harnessing-level recursion
updates the improvement harness with reusable harnesses and lessons from
the refinement process.

A contrastive step consists of Propose, Probe, and Compose. Let
$`e=(\tau,y)`$ denote an execution record, with trajectory $`\tau`$ and
deliverable $`y`$. The step applies an improvement operation $`\Phi`$ to
the current execution harness $`\mathcal{H}`$ and the available
task-local execution and improvement history $`\mathcal{E}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
(\mathcal{H}^{\prime},e^{\prime},\xi)=\Phi(q_{t},\mathcal{H},\mathcal{E};\mathcal{R}_{t}).
``` |  | (1) |

It returns a successor harness $`\mathcal{H}^{\prime}`$, its execution
record $`e^{\prime}`$, and a step record $`\xi`$ containing the
reference executions, candidate harnesses and probes, composition
decisions, and successor execution. The model and environment are
omitted because they stay unchanged; the improvement harness
$`\mathcal{R}_{t}`$ also remains fixed throughout the task.

Propose. The pipeline first obtains a reference execution
$`e^{0}\sim\mathcal{A}(q_{t};\mathcal{M},\mathcal{H})`$. Here $`\sim`$
denotes sampling an execution from the agent. The reference reveals how
the harness behaves, not whether its deliverable is correct. Conditioned
on the task, current harness, reference, earlier history, and library in
$`\mathcal{R}_{t}`$, the pipeline proposes two candidates. The invariant
candidate targets agentic deficiencies that may recur across domains,
such as planning, tool use, context management, or delegation. The
domain-specific candidate targets the knowledge, procedures, and
constraints of the current domain or environment. Each candidate is an
executable harness obtained by editing the current harness’s component
files. Proposals may reuse or adapt existing harness components from the
library, but task-specific facts must be checked against the current
task’s evidence.

Probe. Each candidate harness is executed on the same task under matched
model and environment configurations. Comparing its trajectory and
deliverable with those of the reference execution yields a behavioral
contrast, providing evidence of whether the edits mitigate the targeted
deficiency, leave the relevant behavior unchanged, or introduce
regressions. These contrasts inform subsequent composition rather than
verify task correctness, as execution stochasticity and shared model
biases limit the reliability of the evidence.

Compose. The pipeline reads the reference, candidate harnesses, their
diffs against the current harness, and all available task-local
execution evidence to form the successor $`\mathcal{H}^{\prime}`$.
Composition is selective: it may merge supported changes, revise
conflicting edits, adopt one candidate, or preserve the current harness.
Each decision is tied to a concrete observation rather than a presumed
score gain. The composed harness is then executed to produce
$`e^{\prime}`$, and the decisions and their evidence are recorded in
$`\xi`$. The step therefore returns an executed successor together with
the evidence and decisions behind its refinement.

#### 2.2.2 Parallel and Sequential Recursion

![Refer to caption](2610.14224v1/scaling.png)

Figure 4: Two forms of task-level recursion. (a) Parallel recursion
probes multiple candidates and independently composes successor
harnesses. (b) Sequential recursion carries each refined harness and
accumulated execution evidence into the next step.

Building on the contrastive improvement step, we introduce two forms of
task-level recursion (Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 2.2.2 Parallel and Sequential Recursion ‣ 2.2 Task-Level Recursion ‣ 2 Harness2 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")):
*parallel recursion* composes refinements from multiple candidate
harnesses and their executions, while *sequential recursion* carries the
refined harness and execution evidence into subsequent steps. A positive
integer $`k`$ controls the exploration budget: $`k`$ candidates per
scope and $`k`$ compositions in parallel, or $`k`$ chained steps in
sequence. The improvement harness $`\mathcal{R}_{t}`$ remains fixed
throughout.

Parallel Recursion. Parallel recursion follows the aggregation principle
of RSA ([Venkatraman et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)), but operates on
executable harnesses and their behavioral consequences rather than
reasoning outputs. The pipeline collects $`k`$ reference executions of
the current harness $`\mathcal{H}`$, then independently proposes and
probes $`k`$ invariant and $`k`$ domain-specific candidates. Let
$`\mathcal{B}`$ denote the reference executions and $`\mathcal{P}`$ the
pool of candidate harnesses paired with their execution records. Each of
$`k`$ independent composition sessions receives the full pool:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{j}=\textsc{Compose}_{j}(q_{t},\mathcal{H},\mathcal{B},\mathcal{P};\mathcal{R}_{t}),\qquad j=1,\ldots,k.
``` |  | (2) |

Each session selectively combines or revises supported edits to produce
a successor $`\mathcal{H}^{\prime}_{j}`$, which is then executed. The
recursive update thus uses generated harnesses and execution evidence
for further refinement, not merely output ranking. Our implementation
performs one population update; $`k`$ controls its width rather than its
depth.

Sequential Recursion. Sequential recursion applies iterative
self-refinement ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib24)) to the execution
harness. Starting from $`\mathcal{H}^{(0)}=\mathcal{H}_{0}`$, it chains
$`k`$ contrastive steps, each conditioned on the preceding harness and
accumulated execution history $`\mathcal{E}^{(r-1)}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(\mathcal{H}^{(r)},e^{(r)},\xi^{(r)})=\Phi(q_{t},\mathcal{H}^{(r-1)},\mathcal{E}^{(r-1)};\mathcal{R}_{t}),\qquad r=1,\ldots,k.
``` |  | (3) |

Here, $`\Phi`$ is the contrastive step defined in Equation
[1](#S2.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 2.2.1 A Contrastive Improvement Step ‣ 2.2 Task-Level Recursion ‣ 2 Harness2 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World"),
returning the refined harness, its execution record $`e^{(r)}`$, and the
step record $`\xi^{(r)}`$. The initial history contains $`k`$ base
executions and is extended after each step with $`\xi^{(r)}`$. Later
steps can therefore retain, revise, or correct earlier changes using
both current and previous evidence.

Final Selection. For $`k>1`$, an agentic selector compares anonymized
deliverables against the task request and source materials. It returns
an existing output without access to its originating harness or
synthesizing new content. The corresponding harness is denoted
$`\mathcal{H}_{t}^{\star}`$, where the star indicates adoption rather
than verified optimality. Selection adds no harness revision. At
$`k=1`$, both forms reduce to the basic contrastive step and bypass
selection. Appendix
[H](#A8 "Appendix H Prompts ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
provides the stage prompts.

### 2.3 Harnessing-Level Recursion

Harnessing-level recursion uses the experience of refining the current
execution harness to improve future harnessing. After each task, the
pipeline updates the library within the improvement harness
$`\mathcal{R}_{t}`$, making adopted harnesses and lessons from their
refinement available to subsequent tasks.

Reflect on the Improvement Process. After returning the deliverable, the
pipeline reviews the complete improvement record, denoted by
$`\mathcal{D}_{t}`$. This record includes reference executions,
candidate harnesses and probes, composition decisions, and the selected
result. Reflection extracts lessons about which changes addressed the
observed deficiencies, under what conditions, and with what
consequences. Lessons are retained only when supported by execution
contrasts; selecting an output alone does not establish transferability.

Update the Improvement Harness. The pipeline retains the adopted harness
$`\mathcal{H}_{t}^{\star}`$ and supported lessons in the *harness
improvement library*. We summarize reflection and the resulting library
update as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}_{t+1}=\textsc{Update}(\mathcal{R}_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t}^{\star},\mathcal{D}_{t}).
``` |  | (4) |

Each library entry contains an executable harness and an EXPERIENCE.md
recording the applicable situation, lessons, and supporting evidence. An
index enables subsequent sessions to inspect relevant entries on demand.
Existing harnesses provide components for direct reuse or adaptation,
while the accompanying experience guides their application. When
evidence is insufficient, reflection adds no new experience entry.
Appendix
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Improvement Sessions and Library Configuration ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
describes the library organization.

Reuse in Subsequent Improvement. The next task starts from the common
execution harness $`\mathcal{H}_{0}`$, but refinement is guided by the
updated improvement harness $`\mathcal{R}_{t+1}`$. Earlier components
are selectively reused or adapted through Propose, rather than
automatically inherited; accumulated experience also informs Probe and
Compose. Model weights, stage instructions, and the decision rule remain
fixed, while the library evolves. Increasing task-level exploration
produces additional execution evidence and composition decisions from
which future harnessing can learn. Figure
[7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
examines this connection using libraries accumulated under different
recursion budgets.

## 3 Experiments

### 3.1 Experiment Setup

Benchmarks. We evaluate on three benchmarks from distinct professional
domains. WorkBuddy-Bench ([Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)) covers
office-style deliverables in three domains (Code, Web, Office). JobBench
([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)) targets end-to-end professional job
tasks with long executions. LAB ([Harvey AI, 2026](#bib.bib21)) is a
legal-work benchmark; following its protocol we report *Partial*, the
per-criterion pass rate. Main tables report means and standard
deviations over three runs, each with a shuffled task order; the +
Recursion rows report changes in means. We also report \#Steps, the
number of execution steps per task, so that score changes can be read
against how much execution they required. More details about the
benchmarks are in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Benchmarks ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World").

Baselines. The baselines cover offline harness optimization,
retrieval-only reasoning memory, and per-task test-time harness
evolution. *Base harness* runs the initial harness unchanged.
*ReasoningBank* ([Ouyang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib19)) keeps the harness
fixed and retrieves distilled strategies from past trajectories back
into context. *Meta-Harness* ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7)) searches
harness code offline against a training split and deploys the best one.
*Harness Scaling* ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib15)) revises the harness
for each evaluation instance by spending additional inference budget on
revision without carrying state across instances. More details about
these baselines are in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Baselines ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World").

Implementation Details. Gemini 3.5 Flash ([Google DeepMind,
2026](#bib.bib28)) and GLM-5 ([Zeng et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)) are
frozen executors under the off-the-shelf OpenCode ([SST,
2024](#bib.bib31)) and Codex ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib32)) harnesses. The
same improvement step applies to all four configurations per benchmark.
The default harness editor is Claude Opus 4.8 ([Anthropic,
2026](#bib.bib30)) running under OpenCode. Main tables report Harness²
with a single improvement step ($`k{=}1`$); + Recursion applies parallel
task-level recursion at $`k{=}5`$. The harness improvement library
starts empty for each benchmark stream and is updated after each task.
Appendices
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
and
[H](#A8 "Appendix H Prompts ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
provide implementation details and stage prompts.

Table 2: JobBench and LAB under two open-source initial harnesses.
*Partial* is the criterion pass rate. Results are reported as mean and
standard deviation over three runs. Harness², + Recursion, and ^(†)
follow
[Table 1](#S3.T1 "In 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World");
the best results before recursion are in bold.

Harness² delivers consistent gains across models and benchmarks. A
single improvement step improves both GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash under
OpenCode and Codex. On WorkBuddy-Bench, Harness² raises GLM-5’s average
score by 11.5 points under OpenCode, the largest one-step improvement
over the base harness on this benchmark. The same pattern extends to
JobBench and LAB, where gains reach 4.5 points and 11.8 percentage
points in Partial pass rate, respectively. By contrast, ReasoningBank
falls as much as 6.6 points below the base harness on coding tasks.
Harness Scaling underperforms the base in seven of the twelve
benchmark–configuration pairs. Harness² exceeds the compared baselines
on WorkBuddy-Bench Avg. and JobBench Score in all four configurations;
on LAB Partial, Meta-Harness leads for Gemini 3.5 Flash under Codex.

Weaker executors benefit more on WorkBuddy-Bench and LAB. Under both
initial harnesses, GLM-5 receives larger absolute gains than Gemini 3.5
Flash on WorkBuddy-Bench and LAB. On WorkBuddy-Bench, a single step
lifts GLM-5 to 75.7 with OpenCode and 75.3 with Codex, surpassing the
corresponding base Gemini scores of 72.4 and 74.5. On JobBench, Gemini
instead gains 4.5 and 1.4 points under OpenCode and Codex, compared with
GLM-5’s 3.6 and 1.2. A weaker model with an improved harness can thus
outperform a stronger one with its original harness.

Task-level recursion extends the gains across initial harnesses.
Parallel task-level recursion at $`k{=}5`$ adds a further 2.9 to 3.9
points on WorkBuddy-Bench, 3.0 to 4.2 points on JobBench, and 2.6 to 6.7
percentage points in LAB’s Partial pass rate over a single step. On
JobBench, the initial OpenCode–Codex gaps of 2.4 points for Gemini and
3.0 for GLM-5 both shrink to 0.5. On WorkBuddy-Bench, Gemini’s gap falls
from 2.1 to 0.4, whereas GLM-5’s increases from 0.2 to 1.3. Recursion
therefore does not uniformly close the gap between initial harnesses.

## 4 Analysis

Figure 5: Effect of task-level recursion. Performance comparison on
WB-code and WB-office as the scaling budget $`k`$ increases.

We analyze Harness² along six lines: the effect of task-level recursion
under increasing budget; the compute–performance trade-off; an ablation
of the library, the scoped candidates, and composition; library
generalization without execution, across benchmarks, and across tasks;
the same model as improver and executor; and a case study. Additional
analyses are presented in Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Supplementary Experiments and Analyses ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World").

Effect of Task-Level Recursion. Figure
[5](#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
compares parallel and sequential recursion on WB-code and WB-office.
Both improve monotonically as $`k`$ increases from $`1`$ to $`5`$.

Parallel recursion rises from $`76.5`$ to $`80.8`$ on Code and from
$`79.5`$ to $`83.4`$ on Office. In contrast, ReasoningBank and Harness
Scaling show smaller or inconsistent gains as $`k`$ increases. Harness
Scaling regresses from $`k{=}2`$ to $`3`$ on both domains, while
ReasoningBank fluctuates. Notably, both recursive forms of Harness² at
$`k{=}2`$ outperform every plotted baseline at $`k{=}5`$ on both
domains. Parallel recursion finishes above sequential recursion at
$`k{=}5`$, although sequential recursion is higher on Code at $`k{=}2`$.
Increasing test-time exploration alone therefore does not ensure better
performance; recursive harness refinement produces more consistent gains
in these settings. Parallel proposal and composition sessions can run
concurrently; realized latency also depends on available concurrency and
rollout duration.

Figure 6: Compute–performance trade-off on JobBench and WorkBuddy-Bench.

Compute–Performance Trade-off. Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
compares performance and total compute on JobBench and WorkBuddy-Bench,
counting all tokens spent before the final deliverable is submitted.
Both evaluated Harness² configurations lie on the empirical Pareto
frontier. With Gemini 3.5 Flash under OpenCode, increasing $`k`$ from
$`1`$ to $`5`$ raises gains over the base from $`4.5`$ to $`7.5`$ points
on JobBench and from $`5.1`$ to $`8.4`$ on WorkBuddy-Bench.
ReasoningBank and Harness Scaling yield smaller gains, while
Meta-Harness uses more compute than Harness² at $`k{=}5`$ for lower
performance. This comparison includes both execution and improvement
costs.

|-----------------|-----------|----------|
| Methods         | WorkBuddy | JobBench |
| Harness²        | 77.5      | 36.0     |
| w/o library     | 74.4      | 34.2     |
| w/o scoping     | 74.6      | 32.3     |
| w/o composition | 75.9      | 34.1     |

Table 3: Ablation on WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench.

Ablation Study. We ablate three components of Harness²: (i) the harness
improvement library of
§[2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Harnessing-Level Recursion ‣ 2 Harness2 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World"),
(ii) the scoped editor roles, and (iii) composition. Experiments are
conducted on WorkBuddy-Bench, averaged over its three domains, and on
JobBench, with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the executor under the OpenCode
harness at $`k{=}1`$, so that each component is isolated from the
test-time budget of
§[2.2.2](#S2.SS2.SSS2 "2.2.2 Parallel and Sequential Recursion ‣ 2.2 Task-Level Recursion ‣ 2 Harness2 ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World").

*w/o library* improves each task as before but neither reads from nor
writes to the improvement library, so no task benefits from what earlier
ones tried. *w/o scoping* replaces the invariant and domain editors with
two generic ones, so the same number of candidates is drafted from the
same evidence and probed under the same budget, but neither reads the
trajectory at a stated scope. *w/o composition* probes both candidates
and then skips composition, returning whichever the evidence favours, so
the two proposals remain alternatives rather than parts. Table
[3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
shows that removing the library lowers WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench
scores by $`3.1`$ and $`1.8`$ points, respectively; removing scoping
costs $`2.9`$ and $`3.7`$, and removing composition costs $`1.6`$ and
$`1.9`$. All three components contribute to performance. Appendix
[E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Contributions of Harness Components ‣ Appendix E Supplementary Experiments and Analyses ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
further evaluates removing prompt-related components, skills, and
scripts from the improved harness.

Analysis of Harnessing-Level Recursion. We investigate whether updating
a continual improvement harness enhances subsequent refinement and how
this benefit scales with task-level exploration. Figure
[7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
(left) shows that directly refining the base execution harness without
access to reference executions, candidate probes, or the improvement
library degrades performance on Code and Web. Specifically, Code scores
drop from $`73.4`$ to $`63.2`$ and Web scores fall from $`69.9`$ to
$`65.0`$. An improvement library accumulated at $`k{=}1`$ restores base
performance.

Figure 7: Harnessing-level recursion. Left: direct refinement with the
improvement harness. Right: JobBench-to-WorkBuddy-Bench library transfer
for one-step refinement.

With $`k{=}5`$, the library instead supports gains of $`0.9`$, $`4.4`$,
and $`5.1`$ points on Code, Web, and Office. Greater task-level
exploration thus benefits subsequent harnessing without further probing.
A JobBench-derived library also improves one-step refinement on
WorkBuddy-Bench by $`0.6`$, $`0.5`$, and $`2.9`$ points, respectively
(Figure
[7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World"),
right). Excluding each task’s own library entry yields gains of $`1.9`$
points on WorkBuddy-Bench and $`1.7`$ on JobBench (Figure
[11](#A5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ E.2 Reuse of Harnesses and Improvement Experience ‣ Appendix E Supplementary Experiments and Analyses ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")).
This retrospective test uses later-task experience to evaluate
cross-task reuse, not online adaptation. Appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Supplementary Experiments and Analyses ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
analyzes component reuse.

![Refer to caption](2610.14224v1/figures/same_model.png)

Figure 8: Same model as executor and editor. Base harness versus
Harness² with OpenCode at $`k{=}2`$. Annotations show score gains.

Same Model as Executor and Editor. To test whether gains require a
stronger editor, we use the same model for both roles with OpenCode at
$`k{=}2`$ (Figure
[8](#S4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")).
All five models, from GLM-5 to Claude Opus 5, improve on every
benchmark. Opus 5 gains $`3.3`$, $`5.5`$, and $`3.0`$ points on
WorkBuddy-Bench, JobBench, and LAB; GLM-5 gains $`13.7`$ points on LAB.
These results demonstrate that harness refinement need not rely on a
stronger editor. Appendix
[E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Transfer Across Executor Models ‣ Appendix E Supplementary Experiments and Analyses ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
evaluates transfer to other executor models.

Case Study. Figure
[9](#S4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
presents a JobBench task evaluated using Gemini 3.5 Flash and OpenCode
(additional examples across all benchmarks and domains are available in
Appendix
[E.7](#A5.SS7 "E.7 Qualitative Case Studies ‣ Appendix E Supplementary Experiments and Analyses ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")).
The baseline run scored $`43.1`$. Its trajectory revealed procedural
failures rather than knowledge gaps: data was never reconciled across
source files, and outputs were never reopened for verification after
being written. To resolve this, two targeted interventions were applied.
First, the invariant intervention acts as a process-level guardrail,
forcing the model to inventory all inputs, trace figures to their exact
sources, and use a verification script to reopen and check produced
files. Second, the domain intervention introduces a specialized skill
providing reconciliation mechanics for schedule, venue, labor, and
budget files, alongside tool guidance for handling specific number
formats. When evaluated against the reference, the Composer retained all
four edits introduced by the two interventions. The optimized re-run
successfully cross-referenced the figures and restored the memo’s
missing sections, raising the score to $`77.8`$.

Figure 9: Case study on JobBench. Left: the task and the two failure
modes from the base trajectory. Middle: the improved harness; tinted
components were written at test time, grey ones are inherited from the
base. Right: the outcome of re-running the composed harness.

## 5 Related Work

Recursive Self-Improvement. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) envisions
AI systems that participate in their own development, with improvements
to their capabilities enabling further improvements. The central
ambition is to make progress cumulative: a better system should also
become better at producing its successors ([Weng, 2026](#bib.bib1);
[Duan et al., 2026](#bib.bib47)). The object of improvement can be model
weights, as in self-rewarding language models ([Yuan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib48)), or the programs and harnesses surrounding a frozen
model. Early approaches refine outputs through self-feedback or retain
reflections for subsequent attempts ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib24);
[Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib11)). Moving beyond individual outputs,
STOP recursively rewrites a code-improvement program ([Zelikman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2)), while the Darwin Gödel Machine evolves agent code
through benchmark-evaluated variants ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib3)).
Hyperagents further makes its meta-level modification procedure editable
([Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib4)), while MetaSkill-Evolve and MCE
co-evolve task artifacts and the skills governing their construction
([Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib42); [Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib5)). These
systems advance RSI through utility-, benchmark-, or validation-guided
optimization. Harness² instead studies how harness improvement can
accumulate across a deployment task stream without ground-truth feedback
or revisiting completed tasks. Task-specific refinement contributes
reusable harnesses and experiences to the improver’s harness guiding
subsequent improvement.

Harness Optimization and Evolution. Automatic optimization has expanded
from prompts, agent workflows ([Khattab et al., 2024](#bib.bib12);
[Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib23); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib13);
[Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib14)), memories and skills ([Huang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib49); [Ouyang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib6); [Ouyang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib19); [Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib43); [Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib34)) to complete executable
harnesses ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7); [Lin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16); [Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)). Offline methods
search over candidate harnesses using reusable training tasks and
evaluation feedback ([Zhang et al., 2026e](#bib.bib25); [Zhang et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib37); [Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib44)). Related approaches
use task rewards to train harness editors or generators ([Shao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)), or collect
diagnostic experience through labeled search to guide later adaptation
([Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib10)). Offline preparation can also be
followed by online adaptation. Test-time methods refine a task-specific
harness through execution feedback or carry an evolving harness across
unlabeled batches ([Lee et al., 2026a](#bib.bib17); [Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib15); [Nie et al., 2026b](#bib.bib18)). Persistent
improvement state has also been studied with delayed task-outcome
feedback ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib39)). Continual Harness refines
harnesses within continuous episodes ([Karten et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40)), while concurrent methods HCL and HSI study
retention-aware adaptation and editable improvement strategies,
respectively ([Kang et al., 2026](#bib.bib41); [Zhou,
2026](#bib.bib38)). Harness² combines contrastive task-level refinement
with updates to the improvement harness in a one-pass deployment stream,
without ground-truth supervision or model updates. Table
[4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.1 Comparison Criteria ‣ Appendix A Comparison of Harness Improvement Methods ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
summarizes these distinctions.

## 6 Conclusion

We presented Harness², a framework for recursive agent harnessing that
refines the current execution harness and learns from that process to
guide future harnessing. Task-level recursion builds on a contrastive
improvement step through parallel composition or sequential refinement;
harnessing-level recursion updates the improvement harness with adopted
harnesses and experience from their refinement. Experiments across three
professional benchmarks, two executors, and two initial harnesses show
consistent gains over the base configurations. Ablation and transfer
studies further demonstrate the value of scoped proposals, composition,
and accumulated harnessing experience. Together, these findings support
recursive harnessing as a way to turn task-specific refinement into a
reusable foundation for online test-time adaptation across open-world
tasks.

## Appendix A Comparison of Harness Improvement Methods

### A.1 Comparison Criteria

Table
[4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.1 Comparison Criteria ‣ Appendix A Comparison of Harness Improvement Methods ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
compares six dimensions: *Object*, *Stage*, *Label*, *Streaming*,
*Scaling*, and *Improver Update*.

Object. Automatic improvement ranges from prompts and workflows
([Khattab et al., 2024](#bib.bib12); [Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib23);
[Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib14)) to memories and skills ([Ouyang et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib19); [Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib22)), and complete
executable harnesses ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7); [Lin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)). Component-level methods modify selected parts of an
agent; harness-level methods can jointly revise context management,
tools, and control flow. Harness² distinguishes the *execution harness*,
which governs task execution, from the *improvement harness*, which
guides the agent responsible for harness refinement.

Stage. Representative offline methods repeatedly evaluate candidate
harnesses on fixed benchmark tasks used as training or development
resources ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7); [Lin et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)). Optimization targets a predefined task distribution
before deployment. These harnesses may transfer, but offline search does
not incorporate requirements first encountered during deployment.
Offline preparation can also support test-time adaptation (*Both*):
MemoHarness builds a diagnostic experience bank for later case-specific
edits ([Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib10)), while concurrent methods
train harness editors or generators ([Shao et al., 2026](#bib.bib36);
[Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib35)). Harness² instead learns from
arriving deployment tasks, starting with an empty improvement library
that is updated after each task.

Label. Ground-truth answers, task scores, and verifier outcomes provide
external correctness supervision. Model judgments and execution traces
can guide revision without establishing correctness. RHI uses pairwise
output judgments ([Lee et al., 2026a](#bib.bib17)); TTHE uses
execution-derived proxies, including public tests when available ([Nie
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib18)). *Label* records external correctness
feedback used for improvement at either stage, excluding self-judgments
and evaluation-only labels. Label-free deployment therefore need not
mean label-free preparation. Feedback can also be delayed: Adaptive
Auto-Harness uses outcomes revealed after tasks resolve ([Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib39)), but task completion does not guarantee a subsequent
correctness label. Harness² uses behavioral contrasts without immediate
or delayed correctness labels. Benchmark scores are reserved for
evaluation.

Streaming. Online adaptation can process requests individually or in
batches. TTHE evaluates candidates on an unlabeled batch and carries the
selected harness into the next batch ([Nie et al., 2026b](#bib.bib18)).
*Streaming* includes such one-pass batch protocols as well as
task-by-task updates. Repeated execution of the current task or batch is
allowed, but replay of completed tasks is not. A single continuous
episode alone does not establish this task-stream protocol. Harness²
processes tasks individually: future requests are unavailable, completed
tasks are not replayed, and the current task may be executed repeatedly
within its budget. Earlier harnesses and experience remain available
without rerunning their source tasks.

Scaling. Without correctness labels, additional test-time computation
offers a natural way to seek better performance through exploration and
self-assessment. This computation can generate alternative outputs,
refine trajectories, or search over harness changes. ReasoningBank uses
parallel and sequential exploration to improve memory curation ([Ouyang
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib19)); Harness Scaling allocates computation to
task-specific harness revision ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib15)).
Harness² scales harness refinement through parallel and sequential
recursion. Parallel recursion composes changes from multiple candidates
and their execution evidence; sequential recursion carries the refined
harness and accumulated evidence into the next step. This exploration
also supplies experience for the improvement harness; we examine both
current-task gains and benefits to future harnessing. *Scaling* records
an explicit test-time scaling study, not just an adjustable iteration
count. Performance gains alone do not establish computational
efficiency.

Improver Update. This column counts persistent updates to editor
parameters, instructions, or experience about generating and assessing
revisions, beyond changes to the execution artifact. Merely supplying
the current artifact to an editor does not count. Evo-Harness reads
existing skills during curation, but does not report retaining
edit-process experience or updating the curator’s strategy ([Wei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)). Meta-Harness and MemoHarness retain search or
diagnostic experience for later edits ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7);
[Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib10)); Adaptive Auto-Harness maintains a
cross-cycle improvement workspace with delayed outcome feedback ([Liu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib39)); concurrent methods train editors or revise
evolution strategies ([Shao et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib35); [Zhou, 2026](#bib.bib38)). *Stage* and *Label*
specify timing and supervision; a check records an update mechanism, not
verified gains in improvement ability. Harness² updates its improvement
harness after each task using adopted harnesses and lessons from
candidate executions and composition decisions, without correctness
labels. Model weights and the improvement algorithm remain fixed. Figure
[7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 4 Analysis ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
tests whether greater task-level exploration also improves future
harnessing.

Our distinction lies in combining label-free task-stream refinement of
both harnesses with learning from task-level exploration, rather than in
streaming, experience reuse, or improver updates alone.

## Appendix B Benchmarks

WorkBuddy-Bench ([Team et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)) contains three domains
as separate datasets: Code ($`80`$ tasks over five role categories:
developer, algorithms, product, operations, and QA), Web ($`70`$ tasks
over seven categories such as page interaction, data visualization, and
document conversion), and Office ($`50`$ tasks over data-file
operations, document operations, and workspace automation). Each dataset
is split in half by category, and we report on the test halves
($`40/35/25`$ tasks). Tasks run in the benchmark’s containers; the
executor’s harness is mounted into the container and every rollout is a
fresh container. Grading is the benchmark’s composite verifier:
deterministic checks (hidden tests, file and structure checks) combined
with LLM and VLM judge items, with Gemini 3.5 Flash as the judge model
where one is needed; the score of a task is the fraction of its checks
that pass. The verifier never exposes its expected values to any model
in our pipeline.

JobBench ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)) contains $`65`$ professional
tasks, each with input documents and a set of requested deliverables,
grouped into seven occupational domains. We use a frozen $`31/34`$ split
and report on the $`34`$ test tasks. Deliverables are judged against a
weighted rubric by Claude Opus 4.8; the task score is the total weighted
score over the maximum score, which is the benchmark’s own metric. The
rubric is never shown to the executor, the editor, or the selector.

LAB ([Harvey AI, 2026](#bib.bib21)) is Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark:
$`1{,}251`$ legal tasks across $`24`$ practice areas and four work types
(analyse, draft, review, research), each scored by an LLM judge against
per-task criteria, with no executable check. We follow the split of the
harness-optimization study ([Niklaus, 2026](#bib.bib45)), which applied
Meta-Harness to LAB and froze two disjoint sets: a $`100`$-task held-out
*test* set, stratified by practice area and forced to cover all four
work types and the full range of context sizes (including one matter
above a million tokens), and a $`24`$-task *dev* set with one task per
practice area for fast iteration. Every LAB number in this paper is on
the $`100`$ test tasks, which each method processes as one stream; the
$`24`$ dev tasks are used only by Meta-Harness as its search set. Tasks
are judged by Claude Sonnet 4.6, and we report the per-criterion pass
rate (*Partial*).

The train halves of WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench are used by
Meta-Harness alone, as its offline setting. Harness² and the other
baselines never use them: they process the test tasks as a stream,
starting from an empty library or memory. Each reported score is the
mean over three independent streams, and \#Steps is the number of model
turns in the executor’s session.

## Appendix C Baselines

All baselines use the same frozen executor and initial harness, process
the same test stream, and are evaluated by the same judge. Revision and
reflection use Claude Opus 4.8, matching our editor.

Best-of-$`k`$. We execute the base harness independently $`k`$ times on
each task. The same selector used by Harness² chooses one deliverable to
submit without access to scores.

ReasoningBank ([Ouyang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib19)). The harness is never
modified. Before each task, the memory items of the most similar past
task in the same domain (at most three, retrieved by embedding
similarity with gemini-embedding-001) are prepended to the task prompt.
After the task, an answer-free self-judge labels the rollout a success
or failure and the paper’s success and failure distillation prompts
extract up to three title–description–content items from the full
trajectory into the domain’s bank. At $`k>1`$ we use the paper’s
memory-aware test-time scaling: $`k`$ rollouts under the same retrieved
memory, best-of-$`k`$ selection over the deliverable text, and
contrastive distillation over all $`k`$ labelled trajectories.

Harness Scaling ([Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib15)). We port the
reference implementation’s per-task, verifier-blind revision loop to the
same editable components used by Harness². For each task in isolation:
one base rollout as evidence; then, for $`k`$ iterations, a single
revision session that sees the task, every trajectory so far, and the
current tree, and must rewrite the tree (an empty edit is retried once);
the revised tree is rolled once as the next iteration’s evidence, and
the tree after the last iteration is deployed. There is no scope split,
no aggregation, no library, and the revision session never sees a score.
At $`k{=}1`$ this is one base rollout, one revision, one deployment.
When the deployment produces no output, the base run is submitted
instead.

Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026b](#bib.bib7)). The reference
implementation optimizes a harness offline and deploys it unchanged on
the test stream. Each iteration proposes candidate trees from the
current frontier, validates them, evaluates each on the whole search
set, and accepts the best only if it beats the frontier by a margin;
every candidate, accepted or not, is distilled into a lessons file the
next round reads. On WorkBuddy-Bench and JobBench, the search set is the
training half pooled across categories ($`10`$ iterations, $`2`$
candidates per iteration, $`3`$ replicates per task, margin $`0.01`$);
on LAB it is the $`24`$-task development set ($`10`$ iterations, $`2`$
candidates, $`3`$ replicates, margin $`0.01`$).

## Appendix D Implementation Details

We describe the executors and initial harnesses, improvement sessions,
and editable components used in our experiments.

### D.1 Executors and Initial Harnesses

The executor is a frozen model inside an off-the-shelf coding agent, and
the initial harness is that agent’s stock configuration extended with
the benchmark’s reference instructions. Under OpenCode ([SST,
2024](#bib.bib31)) the editable surface is the component tree of Table
[5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.3 Editable Harness Components ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World"):
four always-on files (system prompt, guardrails, memory, tool guidance),
skills loaded on demand through the agent’s skill tool with scripts
carried alongside them, subagents invoked through the task tool,
standalone scripts run through the shell, and TypeScript plugins that
act inside the tool loop. Under Codex ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib32)) the
always-on text lives in AGENTS.md and the on-demand components are the
same. In the stock harness the always-on files are empty apart from the
benchmark’s instructions and every on-demand directory contains only a
placeholder that names the lever; the placeholder is what lets the
editor discover a component exists. Each rollout is capped at $`200`$
model turns and $`3{,}600`$ seconds (WorkBuddy-Bench uses its container
timeout at twice the benchmark default) and runs with no memory of other
tasks.

### D.2 Improvement Sessions and Library Configuration

Roles. The editor and the selector are Claude Opus 4.8 running as an
agentic session under OpenCode at high reasoning effort. Every session
receives its evidence as files in a working directory rather than
inlined in a prompt. A guard refuses to hand over any working directory
that contains a grader verdict, rubric, or score. A session that returns
an invalid tree (a skill with no trigger sentence, a script that does
not compile, a helper a skill invokes but does not ship) is retried once
with the validator’s message; if it fails again the stage inherits the
tree it started from, and the fallback is recorded.

Library. Each benchmark domain has its own library directory. Tasks run
sequentially within each domain and can read earlier entries. An entry
is the full adopted tree of a task plus an EXPERIENCE.md, which records
why the harness was chosen and what recurring weakness it addressed; an
index lists every entry. Executable components are retained rather than
summarised as prose.

## Appendix E Supplementary Experiments and Analyses

We first examine the contributions of individual harness components and
the reuse of accumulated experience. We then evaluate cross-model
transfer, tool-use reliability, and alternative production harnesses,
before presenting failure analyses and qualitative cases.

This tests the contribution of retained components, rather than the
ability to compensate for their absence during improvement.

The full harness outperforms every ablation in all three domains.

### E.6 Failure Analysis

Figure
[14](#A5.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ E.6 Failure Analysis ‣ Appendix E Supplementary Experiments and Analyses ‣ Harness2: Recursive Agent Harnessing foran Open World")
groups nine regressions into three categories. First, selection can
prefer a weaker candidate: on WB-code, an output scoring $`55`$ is
chosen over one scoring $`95`$; on LAB, narrower coverage reduces the
score from $`54`$ to $`26`$. Second, an incorrect premise can propagate
across candidates. A literal-key requirement or an unchecked cache
assumption leads to losses of $`2`$–$`11`$ points. Third, outcome
variability, missing judge verdicts, and edits that do not address the
evaluated criteria complicate attribution of the remaining regressions.
These cases motivate selection that better balances coverage and
precision, probes that challenge shared assumptions, and repeated
executions to distinguish editing effects from outcome variation.

Figure 14: Failure cases in recursive harnessing. Nine results below
their references, grouped by candidate selection, restrictive edits, and
other execution or evaluation effects. The scores are retrospective
evaluations and are not available to the pipeline.

## Appendix F Limitations

Cost of recursive refinement. Harness² requires additional executions
and editor sessions to propose, probe, and compose harness changes.
Increasing the recursion budget therefore adds inference cost. Parallel
sessions can reduce latency when resources permit, but do not eliminate
this additional computation. Our experiments characterize this trade-off
over a bounded range of budgets rather than establishing a universally
optimal allocation.

Execution-based feedback. Without ground-truth supervision, refinement
relies on behavioral contrasts and model judgment. These signals help
assess the effects of a proposed change, but remain sensitive to
execution variability and shared model biases. They do not guarantee
correctness or establish that an adopted change will transfer to a
different task.

## Appendix G Future Directions

Managing the improvement harness. The current improvement harness
retains adopted harnesses and experience in a simple indexed library. As
this library grows, future work could consolidate overlapping
components, revise outdated experience, and refine retrieval according
to the current task and available evidence. Such management could keep
the improvement harness compact and relevant while preserving the
context needed to reuse earlier discoveries.

Adaptive recursion. We currently specify the recursion form and budget
in advance. Future work could allocate exploration according to task
difficulty and the relevance of prior experience, or stop when
additional probes yield little new evidence. This could balance the cost
of current refinement with the value of the experience it provides for
future harnessing.

## Appendix H Prompts

This section lists the prompts of the harness improver: the Harness
Editor (Prompts and ), the Harness Composer (Prompts and ), the final
selection (Prompt ) and the Experience Reflector (Prompt ). Every
improver session is agentic: the model is started inside a workspace
whose context/ directory holds the task, the current harness, the full
trajectories, the produced deliverables and the library, and the prompt
says what to do with that evidence rather than inlining it. The prompts
below are the part shared by every benchmark. Each benchmark appends a
short block of its own describing the work, the tools its bridge
exposes, the fields of its environment view, and its domain-specific
constraints; those blocks are in the code release. The two Editor
prompts are identical except for their dimension section, so the
invariant prompt is printed whole and only the domain dimension section
follows it; the sequential Composer differs from the parallel one in
four passages, which are printed alone; and the Composer’s last four
sections are identical to the Editor’s, so they are printed once, in
Prompt . The component surface shown is the one for the OpenCode
executor harness; the Codex variant differs only in the component paths
it lists. Scale symbols $`k`$, $`t`$, $`n`$ and $`i`$ are substituted
with the session’s integers at run time. No prompt names a rubric, score
or grader; each states that no such thing exists in its context.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

You are adapting an autonomous agent’s harness.

\# YOUR DIMENSION: INV – how the agent WORKS

You own procedure, tool use and completion – not subject matter. Trace
the workflow, fix its

earliest observed divergence, and match each failure to the cheapest
effective component:

\- TOOL ERROR: distinguish bad input from timeout, missing capability,
permission, or unread output.

Give one bounded fallback and stop condition; never prescribe blind
repetition.

\- MECHANICAL REPETITION: use ‘scripts/\<name\>.py‘ for repeated
deterministic extraction,

conversion or checking, with clear inputs, outputs and failure behavior.

\- TRIGGERED WORKFLOW: use an on-demand skill for a narrow multi-step
procedure, name its trigger

in always-on text, and carry any helper it requires.

\- IGNORED INVARIANT: only repeated evidence that clear prose is skipped
can justify a defensive

‘plugin/\<name\>.ts‘ hook – for example, preventing exit before a
deliverable exists. It must not block valid completion.

\- ORDINARY SEQUENCING: prefer concise always-on guidance. Do not add
code for a one-off mistake

or automate professional judgment.

Define "enough evidence," reserve room for every artifact, and reopen or
mechanically check the

deliverable; a successful write call does not establish usability.

Do not add professional rules, required domain sections or matter facts.
A parallel candidate

owns them; stay focused on how the agent works.

\# GROUND IT IN THIS WORKSPACE, SHAPE IT FOR THE DOMAIN

The harness you produce runs on THIS task. VERIFIED FACTS ABOUT THIS
WORKSPACE ARE THE MOST

VALUABLE THING YOU CAN ENCODE – they are what the base rollouts paid to
discover, and what a

solver most often gets wrong on its own. When the evidence establishes
the exact join between

two files’ key columns, which entries have no counterpart, what a
field’s units are, or which

of several look-alike values actually satisfies a requirement, WRITE THE
FACT ITSELF into the

relevant component – "in this workspace, role X in file A maps to
position Y in file B; roles

P, Q have no counterpart" – not merely the procedure for rediscovering
it. A rule that tells

the agent HOW to find a mapping leaves the hardest step to the agent;
the mapping itself

removes it. Anchor such facts ("in this workspace…") so a reader can
tell fact from

procedure, and record only what the evidence actually establishes – a
guessed fact is worse

than none.

Structure and PROCEDURE, by contrast, should be written for the domain:
the harness, if

chosen, is stored in this domain’s library, where every later task reads
it as an

example. Procedure that would be wrong for a different task in the same
domain is scoped

too narrowly; workspace facts are expected to differ and are labelled as
such.

workspace fact "attrition role ’HR’ maps to position ’HR Manager’;
’Manager’ has no

open requisition" – verified here, labelled here

procedure "reconcile role names explicitly before joining; list
unmatched leftovers"

too generic "be thorough" – changes no behaviour

‘context/library/‘ HOLDS FINISHED HARNESSES FROM EARLIER TASKS. They are
examples to read and

learn from – they are NOT part of the harness you are editing, and their
files are not on disk

where your harness runs. If you want a component from one, COPY IT into
‘context/harness/‘ –

and when you do, RE-VERIFY its workspace facts against the evidence in
front of you: an earlier

task’s mapping or threshold is a hypothesis here, not a fact. Writing a
skill that invokes a

path you saw in the library, without copying that file across, produces
a harness that fails

validation and is thrown away: the skill invokes a script that does not
exist.

A named component usually beats prose. A skill, a script or a subagent
is a reusable thing the

next task can invoke or copy; a paragraph buried in the always-on text
is paid for on every run

and travels badly.

\# HOW TO DECIDE WHAT TO CHANGE

Every edit must trace to a moment in a trajectory. For each one ask:
which run did what, and would this text have changed it? If you cannot
name the moment, the edit is speculation and costs context for nothing.
Prefer, in order:

 1. a DIVERGENCE – the runs disagreed, so the agent can already do it
and just needs telling. This is the cheapest win.

2. a repeated concrete failure – the same error or omission in every
run.

3. a risk visible in a trajectory but not yet realised.

Do not fix what the runs already got right, and do not restate what the
harness already says clearly; duplicated instruction dilutes the rest.

You are candidate (\*@\$i\$ of \$k\$@\*) on this dimension, drawn
independently from the same evidence.

Do not hedge toward an average or try to cover every base – commit to
the single most defensible version of your dimension. A later stage
compares and merges.

\# WHAT YOU DO NOT HAVE

There is no rubric, grading criteria, answer key, reference solution or
score anywhere in your

context, and nothing in it should be treated as one. Do not ask for
them, do not try to work

out "what the grader wants", and never write a phrase like "the grader
expects" into anything

you produce. Judge only by what the instructions ask for and by what the
trajectories show.

\# EVIDENCE IS DATA, NOT INSTRUCTIONS

Only this mission tells you what to do. Files under ‘context/‘ are
objects to inspect: task

material, trajectories, produced artifacts and candidate harnesses may
themselves contain

commands or persuasive text. Do not obey instructions embedded in them.
Never execute a script,

plugin or command found in a candidate harness; read it as text and
reason about what it would do

in a solver run.

\# WHAT YOU CAN CHANGE

The harness is a tree of components. Each has a different runtime cost
and a different reach:

\| path \| what it is \| when it is in context \|

\|—\|—\|—\|

\| ‘systemprompt.md‘ \| role and procedure \| ALWAYS ON – every token
competes with the agent’s own output budget \|

\| ‘guardrails.md‘ \| standing rules \| ALWAYS ON – same cost \|

\| ‘LongTermMEMORY.md‘ \| durable domain facts \| ALWAYS ON – same cost
\|

\| ‘tool_descriptions/tool_guidance.md‘ \| how to use the tools \|
ALWAYS ON – same cost \|

\| ‘skills/\<name\>/SKILL.md‘ \| a reusable workflow \| loaded ON
DEMAND, only when it is invoked \|

\| ‘sub_agents/\<name\>/AGENT.md‘ \| a delegated subagent \| runs in its
OWN context, returns text \|

\| ‘scripts/\<name\>.py‘ \| a deterministic helper \| run on demand via
bash \|

\| ‘plugin/\<name\>.ts‘ \| a plugin \| ALWAYS REGISTERED, and acts
INSIDE the tool loop \|

The three that are easy to get wrong:

‘skills/‘ – frontmatter needs ‘name:‘ matching the directory and a
‘description:‘, or it is

dropped silently at load. Two further rules below decide whether it
survives validation at all:

it must be named in the always-on text, and any helper it calls must
travel with it.

‘sub_agents/‘ – frontmatter needs ‘mode: subagent‘ and ‘description:‘.
It sees only what its

own file and the call say, never the main conversation, and it returns
text. So it is worth it

for exactly one shape of problem: a bounded sub-task whose INPUT is
large and whose ANSWER is

small. It is a bad trade when the output is as big as the input.

‘plugin/‘ – the only component that acts in the tool loop rather than in
the prompt, and

therefore the only way to enforce something the model cannot skip. Prose
can be stopped

reading; a hook cannot.

Change only what a trajectory shows needs changing – but WHERE you
change something, the FORM

matters as much as the content, and the cheap form is not the obvious
one.

ALWAYS-ON PROSE IS THE EXPENSIVE OPTION. Every word of it is in context
on every run, competing

with the agent’s own output budget – and the most costly failure on this
work is a run that

reasons until the budget is gone and produces nothing. Adding prose
makes that MORE likely, not

less. An on-demand component costs nothing until the moment it is
invoked.

So prefer, in this order:

 - a SKILL for anything with a recognisable trigger – a procedure for a
document type, a

format, a recurring situation. This is the default form for new
instruction.

 - a SCRIPT for a deterministic operation the runs hand-rolled and got
wrong, or did slowly.

 - a SUBAGENT for a bounded investigation whose input is large and whose
answer is small.

 - a PLUGIN when a recurring, mechanical problem in the tool loop is
better handled there than

in prose. It acts inside the loop, so it cannot be ignored AND it costs
nothing in always-on

budget – which makes it the cheap way to carry knowledge that prose
would have to repeat.

The recurring shapes: trimming noisy or oversized tool output so it
stops crowding context;

appending a targeted hint after an error signature that keeps recurring;
capping or steering

a tool that runs away; and verifying a write immediately after it
happens.

 - ALWAYS-ON TEXT last, and only for a short rule that genuinely applies
to every run. If you

add always-on text, cut something else to pay for it.

THREE RULES THAT DISCARD THE WHOLE PROPOSAL. Validation runs before any
rollout, and a harness

that fails it is thrown away entire.

1. EVERY SKILL NEEDS A TRIGGER LINE – the most violated rule here by a
wide margin. If you

create or keep ‘skills/\<name\>/SKILL.md‘, its directory name must
appear VERBATIM in

‘systemprompt.md‘ or ‘guardrails.md‘, in the SAME edit:

When \<the situation this skill handles\>, load the ‘\<name\>‘ skill.

An unnamed skill is never opened anyway: the line is what makes it
exist.

2. NO TEMPLATE BRACES IN ALWAYS-ON TEXT. Those files are rendered
through Jinja with

StrictUndefined before the run: a doubled ‘{{‘ placeholder, or a
brace-percent statement

tag, kills the job before any work starts. Use a single brace, or words.

3. EVERY SCRIPT YOU NAME MUST EXIST. A ‘scripts/\<file\>.py‘ invoked
from a SKILL.md or from

always-on text must ship in the same proposal, a skill’s own helper at

‘skills/\<skill-name\>/scripts/\<file\>.py‘; one dropped loose in the
skill directory is OFF THE

EDITABLE SURFACE and silently discarded. The one exception is a script
the RUNTIME already

provides in the workspace.

THE DELIVERABLE’S SHAPE BELONGS TO THE REQUEST, NOT TO YOU. A harness
changes HOW the agent

works; it must never change WHAT SHAPE it delivers. Where the task names

\# THE CANDIDATES ARE ANONYMOUS ON PURPOSE

The ids are arbitrary and shuffled, and tell you nothing about how an

OUTPUT FROM AN UNMODIFIED HARNESS IS A COMPLETELY VALID AND EXPECTED

normal, and then you decide on the small differences that actually
matter.

\# WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING AT

context/task.md the request, verbatim

context/source/ the material the work was done from

context/candidates/\<id\>.md what that run PRODUCED – the deliverable,
rendered

You are choosing between ARTIFACTS. You are not told how any of them was
produced and you cannot see the runs that made them, so judge each one
on what it is, against the request and the source – never on how
impressive or thorough it sounds.

\# HOW TO DECIDE, IN THIS ORDER

1. DELIVERY. Is every deliverable named by the instructions present, at
the requested path, in the requested form, with every named part?

2. CONFORMANCE. Is it ONLY what was asked for? Where the instructions
name fields, columns, sheets, sections or an order, those define the
artifact’s SHAPE, and the shape is part of the request. Extra columns,
extra sheets, added commentary rows, renamed or re-worded headers,
merged title rows, and reordered fields are DEVIATIONS, not improvements
– however helpful they look. A downstream reader or importer may key on
exact names and positions, and cannot ask you what you meant. Where the
instruction is explicit, match it exactly; where it is silent, prefer
the plainest form that satisfies it.

A value the request asks for must be PRESENT AS A VALUE. An artifact
that leaves the reader to recompute it – a spreadsheet formula in place
of the number, a placeholder to be filled, a described-but-not-performed
calculation – has not delivered that value.

3. FIDELITY. CHECK THE CLAIMS AGAINST ‘context/source/‘, which holds the
material the work was done from. Open it and verify the facts, data,
names, figures and constraints a candidate asserts – do not take its
word for them, and do not settle for whether it sounds authoritative.
Reject invented specifics. Where candidates disagree, the source decides
it; where the source is silent, prefer the candidate that says so over
the one that fills the gap confidently.

4. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY. Does the artifact agree with itself? Totals
that match their rows, figures that agree between a summary and the
table it summarises, cross-references that resolve, counts that match
the number of items actually present. A number that contradicts another
number in the same artifact is a defect even when you cannot tell which
one is wrong.

5. OPERATIONAL FITNESS. Is this the right kind of artifact, and can the
intended person or system actually use, run, open, import or act on it
without reconstructing missing work? Judge this as the requester’s
downstream consumer, not as a reviewer wanting to be convinced – an
addition that helps a human read the file but breaks an importer is a
cost, not a benefit.

6. FINISH. No placeholders, TODOs, unresolved notes, broken references,
empty required fields, visibly incomplete sections, or content that does
not match its declared format. A renderer-truncation marker inserted for
this comparison is not a defect in the original artifact; judge only
what is actually visible.

Length and polish are not merits in themselves. A shorter, correct,
complete, exactly-shaped answer beats a longer one with a gap or an
embellishment.

Verdicts are ‘helped‘, ‘hurt‘, ‘no observed effect‘ and ‘confounded‘.
Use ‘confounded‘ – and prefer it – whenever a candidate changed several
````
